Design your workload to withstand component failures
Hardware faults, software defects, network partitions, and the loss
    of an Availability Zone may all occur in normal operation. Design
    each workload to expect these failures and keep serving customers
    when they happen, rather than assuming its components stay healthy.
This capability covers how an organization designs a workload to
    keep running when its components fail: detecting faults at every
    layer, failing over to healthy resources, automating recovery so it
    does not wait for a person, keeping recovery actions on the most
    available paths, holding capacity in advance for static stability,
    notifying teams even when automation resolves an event, and
    designing to the availability target the business set.
REL11: How do you design your workload to withstand
            component failures?
REL11-BP01 Monitor all components of the workload to detect failures
REL11-BP02 Fail over to healthy resources
REL11-BP03 Automate healing on all layers
REL11-BP04 Rely on the data plane and not the control plane during recovery
REL11-BP05 Use static stability to prevent bimodal behavior
REL11-BP06 Send notifications when events impact availability
REL11-BP07 Architect your product to meet availability targets and uptime service level agreements (SLAs)
Capability intent
Every layer of the workload is monitored, so a fault is
          detected within the recovery time the workload must meet.
Load is spread across independent resources, Availability
          Zones, or Regions, and traffic shifts away from an impairment
          automatically where the service allows.
Recovery runs through automation rather than manual runbooks,
          and leans on data plane operations that stay available during
          large events.
Capacity to absorb a failure is provisioned before the
          failure, so the workload behaves the same whether or not a
          component is impaired.
Notifications reach the right teams whenever availability is
          affected, including the faults that automated healing quietly
          resolves.
Each workload has an explicit availability target, set during
          design, that drives its architecture and its dependency
          choices.
Common issues to watch for
Monitoring covers only customer-facing interfaces, so gray
          failures in the layers beneath serve slow or wrong results
          while health checks still report healthy.
Failover is designed but never rehearsed, so quotas, stale
          configuration, or missing capacity in the recovery location
          block it during a real event.
Recovery depends on control plane operations, such as creating
          resources or editing DNS records, which are the operations
          most likely to be degraded during a large impairment.
Workloads try to acquire capacity at the moment of failure
          rather than holding it in advance, so recovery fails exactly
          when spare capacity and the control plane are least certain.
Automated healing resolves a recurring fault silently, so no
          one fixes the root cause and the failure keeps happening.
Workloads are built without an availability target, so there
          is no basis for the architectural trade-offs that determine
          whether they can meet one.
